artifacts.title: Tel Dan Stele
artifacts.description: Aramaic inscription by an Aramean king (likely Hazael of Damascus) mentioning the 'House of David' and the 'King of Israel'.
artifacts.significance: Earliest known reference to the House of David outside the Bible.

artifacts.title: Zakkur Stele
artifacts.description: Royal inscription of King Zakkur of Hamath and Lu'ash, describing his victory over a coalition led by Bar-Hadad of Aram-Damascus.
artifacts.significance: Important source for Aramean political history and the Aramaic language.

artifacts.title: Sefire Stelae
artifacts.museum: Damascus National Museum / National Museum of Beirut
artifacts.description: Three basalt stelae containing an Aramaic treaty between Mati'el of Arpad (Bit-Agusi) and Bar-Ga'yah of KTK.
artifacts.significance: Longest known Old Aramaic inscription. Key source for Aramaic treaty language and diplomacy.

artifacts.title: Tell Halaf Sculptures
artifacts.description: Monumental stone sculptures including lions, sphinxes, and relief orthostats from the palace of Kapara, ruler of Bit-Bahiani.
artifacts.significance: Major example of Aramean monumental art blending Syro-Hittite and Mesopotamian styles.

artifacts.title: Hadad-yith'i Bilingual (Tell Fekheriye)
artifacts.description: Bilingual Assyrian-Aramaic inscription on a statue dedicated to the storm god Hadad by an Aramean governor of Guzana.
artifacts.significance: One of the earliest known Aramaic inscriptions and key evidence for early Aramaic script development.

artifacts.title: Kilamuwa Stele
artifacts.description: Royal stele of King Kilamuwa of Bit-Gabbar depicting the king in royal attire with a Phoenician inscription describing his achievements.
artifacts.significance: Documents the political history of Bit-Gabbar and its relations with Assyria.

artifacts.title: Panamuwa I Inscription (Hadad Statue)
artifacts.description: Inscription in Samalian Aramaic on a statue of the storm god Hadad, erected by King Panamuwa I of Bit-Gabbar.
artifacts.significance: Key source for the Samalian dialect and Aramean religious practices.

artifacts.title: Panamuwa II Inscription
artifacts.description: Funerary inscription in Samalian Aramaic erected by Bar-Rakib to honor his father Panamuwa II, who died during Tiglath-Pileser III's campaign against Damascus.
artifacts.significance: Key source for the Samalian dialect and the political history of Bit-Gabbar.

artifacts.title: Bar-Rakib Inscriptions
artifacts.description: Multiple inscriptions of King Bar-Rakib of Bit-Gabbar, written in Imperial Aramaic rather than the local Samalian dialect.
artifacts.significance: Among the earliest records using Imperial Aramaic, showing the spread of standardized Aramaic.

artifacts.title: Katumuwa Stele
artifacts.description: Funerary stele of a royal official named Katumuwa, with an Aramaic inscription describing mortuary rituals and the soul's dwelling in the stele.
artifacts.significance: Unique evidence for Aramean beliefs about the afterlife and soul.

artifacts.title: Kilamuwa Scepter
artifacts.description: Inscribed scepter belonging to King Kilamuwa of Bit-Gabbar.
artifacts.significance: Royal artifact demonstrating the material culture of Aramean kingship.

artifacts.title: Hazael Booty Inscriptions
artifacts.description: Ivory pieces inscribed with the name of Hazael, king of Aram-Damascus, found at the Assyrian provincial capital of Arslan Tash.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of the wealth and reach of Aram-Damascus under Hazael.

artifacts.title: Hazael Horse Frontlet
artifacts.description: Bronze horse frontlet inscribed with the name of Hazael, king of Aram-Damascus, found at the Heraion of Samos.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramean diplomatic or trade connections reaching the Aegean world.

artifacts.title: Melqart Stele
artifacts.description: Basalt stele erected by Bar-Hadad, king of Aram, dedicated to the god Melqart. Contains an Aramaic inscription.
artifacts.significance: Important evidence for Aramean royal dedications and religious practices.

artifacts.title: Arslan Tash Amulets
artifacts.description: Small limestone amulets with Aramaic incantation texts against demons and evil spirits.
artifacts.significance: Rare evidence of Aramean magical and religious practices.

artifacts.title: Arslan Tash Ivory Inscription
artifacts.description: Inscribed ivory piece found at Arslan Tash (ancient Hadatu), capital of Bit-Adini after Assyrian conquest.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramean artistic production and luxury goods.

artifacts.title: Til Barsip Wall Paintings
artifacts.description: Polychrome wall paintings from the palace at Til Barsip, capital of Bit-Adini, showing military scenes and court life.
artifacts.significance: Rare surviving examples of ancient Near Eastern wall painting from an Aramean capital.

artifacts.title: Hamath Inscriptions
artifacts.description: Multiple stone inscriptions in Luwian hieroglyphs and Aramaic from the kingdom of Hamath, documenting its rulers.
artifacts.significance: Shows the bilingual nature of the Hamath kingdom and Aramean cultural influence.

artifacts.title: Hama Graffiti
artifacts.description: Aramaic graffiti found during excavations at Hama (ancient Hamath), including short texts and names.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of everyday Aramaic use in the kingdom of Hamath.

artifacts.title: Tell Halaf Bit-Hilani Palace
artifacts.description: Remains of a monumental bit-hilani palace with carved basalt orthostats, caryatid figures, and a scorpion gate.
artifacts.significance: Best-preserved example of Aramean palatial architecture.

artifacts.title: Tell Halaf Inscription
artifacts.description: Aramaic inscription from Tell Halaf, destroyed during World War II bombing of Berlin.
artifacts.significance: Lost artifact documenting Aramean presence at Guzana.

artifacts.title: Bukan Stele
artifacts.description: Aramaic inscription found in western Iran, one of the easternmost Old Aramaic texts discovered.
artifacts.significance: Demonstrates the spread of Aramaic language and culture far beyond the Levant.

artifacts.title: Neirab Steles
artifacts.description: Two funerary steles with Aramaic inscriptions from the village of Neirab near Aleppo, depicting priests of the moon god.
artifacts.significance: Important evidence for Aramean funerary practices and religious beliefs.

artifacts.title: Tayma Stones
artifacts.description: Aramaic inscriptions found at the oasis of Tayma in northwestern Arabia, dating to the Persian period.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramaic use in the Arabian Peninsula during the Achaemenid period.

artifacts.title: Assur Ostracon and Tablets
artifacts.description: Aramaic ostraca and clay tablets found at the ancient Assyrian capital of Assur, showing administrative use of Aramaic.
artifacts.significance: Evidence that Aramaic was used alongside Akkadian in Assyrian administration.

artifacts.title: Saqqara Aramaic Stele
artifacts.description: Aramaic funerary stele found at Saqqara in Egypt, dating to the Persian period.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramean presence in Egypt during the Achaemenid period.

artifacts.title: Elephantine Papyri
artifacts.museum: Various (Brooklyn Museum, Cairo Museum, Bodleian Library)
artifacts.description: Large collection of Aramaic papyri from a Jewish-Aramean military colony on Elephantine island in the Nile.
artifacts.significance: Major source for Imperial Aramaic and daily life in the Persian Empire.

artifacts.title: Hermopolis Aramaic Papyri
artifacts.description: Eight Aramaic letters found at Hermopolis in Egypt, containing personal correspondence.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramaic-speaking communities in Egypt and their social networks.

artifacts.title: Sarıaydın Inscription
artifacts.description: Aramaic rock inscription in Cilicia (southern Turkey), dating to the Persian period.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramaic use in Anatolia during the Achaemenid period.

artifacts.title: Daskyleion Steles
artifacts.museum: Museum of the Ancient Orient, Istanbul
artifacts.description: Aramaic funerary steles found at Daskyleion, the satrapal capital of Hellespontine Phrygia.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramaic as the administrative language of the Persian Empire in western Anatolia.

artifacts.title: Luristan Aramaic Inscriptions
artifacts.description: Aramaic inscriptions found in the Luristan region of western Iran.
artifacts.significance: Evidence of Aramaic penetration into the Iranian highlands.

artifacts.title: Kandahar Bilingual Rock Inscription
artifacts.description: Bilingual Greek-Aramaic rock inscription of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, proclaiming Buddhist principles.
artifacts.significance: Demonstrates Aramaic as a language of international communication reaching Central Asia.

artifacts.title: Aramaic Inscription of Taxila
artifacts.description: Aramaic inscription found at the ancient city of Taxila in modern Pakistan.
artifacts.significance: Easternmost known Aramaic inscription, showing the language's reach to the Indian subcontinent.

artifacts.title: Pul-i-Darunteh Inscription
artifacts.description: Aramaic rock inscription of Ashoka found near Jalalabad in Afghanistan.
artifacts.significance: Further evidence of Aramaic use in the Mauryan Empire's western provinces.

artifacts.title: Bactria Aramaic Documents
artifacts.description: Collection of Aramaic administrative documents from Bactria, dating to the late Achaemenid period.
artifacts.significance: Shows Aramaic functioning as the bureaucratic language of the Persian Empire in Central Asia.

artifacts.title: Aramaic Inscription of Laghman
artifacts.description: Aramaic rock inscription of Ashoka found in the Laghman valley of Afghanistan.
artifacts.significance: Part of the Ashokan edicts demonstrating Aramaic's role as a lingua franca in the East.

artifacts.title: Palmyrene Inscriptions
artifacts.description: Over 3,500 inscriptions in Palmyrene Aramaic from the ancient city of Palmyra, covering trade, religion, and civic life.
artifacts.significance: Largest corpus of Aramaic inscriptions from a single site. Documents Aramean culture in the Roman period.
